entities.name: Alvise Cadamosto
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alvise Cadamosto, a Venetian navigator born around 1432, emerged as a pivotal figure in the early Portuguese maritime expansion, undertaking two groundbreaking voyages to West Africa in 1455 and 1456 under the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator. His expeditions significantly extended the known European reach along the African coast, documenting new territories, peoples, and commercial opportunities, including the burgeoning trade in enslaved Africans. Cadamosto’s detailed accounts provided an unprecedented glimpse into West African societies and geography, making him a crucial chronicler of the nascent Age of Discovery.

Between 1455 and 1456, Cadamosto, often accompanied by the Genoese captain Antoniotto Usodimare, sailed from Lagos, Portugal. His first voyage in 1455 navigated past the Senegal River and explored the Gambia River, establishing contact with local rulers and engaging in trade for gold, ivory, and enslaved people. The subsequent expedition in 1456 pushed even further south, possibly reaching the Geba River in present-day Guinea-Bissau. During this second journey, Cadamosto and his crew are credited with the discovery of several islands in the Cape Verde archipelago, marking a significant geographical achievement and the greatest leap in Portuguese exploration since 1446.

Cadamosto's most enduring contribution was his meticulously detailed narrative, *Navigazione di Alvise Cadamosto*, published posthumously. This work became an indispensable resource for European cartographers, merchants, and subsequent explorers, offering invaluable insights into the hydrography, ethnography, and commercial potential of West Africa. His reports not only fueled further Portuguese expansion along the African coast but also solidified the economic rationale for the Atlantic slave trade, influencing the strategic understanding that would facilitate future voyages around the Cape of Good Hope and ultimately reshape global commerce and demographics.
